newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Japan says trade insurance plan to get OK at APEC.
newsitem.headline: Japan says trade insurance plan to get OK at APEC.

text.p: Japan's Trade Minister Shinji Sato said on Friday Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) members had basically agreed to Tokyo's proposal that trade insurance agencies help boost private sector development of infrastructure.
"There is a growing consensus among APEC members on the trade insurance scheme," Sato, Japan's minister for international trade and industry, told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
Sato is attending the two-day ministerial meeting of the APEC forum which started on Friday. The meeting culminates with a summit scheduled for Monday at Subic Bay outside Manila.

Trade insurance is one of Japan's main proposals at this year's APEC meeting, the others being private sector involvement in future action plans to free trade and investment by individual APEC members, and drafting a set of guidelines for protecting foreign investment.
"The trade insurance scheme will most possibly make it into the ministerial statement (to be issued on Saturday)," Sato said.
Business leaders at an APEC Business Forum coinciding with the APEC conference said earlier that political risk was a big factor inhibiting vital private investment for infrastructure projects.
The World Bank estimates that East Asia alone will need an infusion of some $1.5 trillion of infrastructure investment by the year 2004.
Sato told business leaders at the forum that around 30 percent of this demand would need to be met through private sector investment.
He called for a network to be established across the Pacific Rim to support trade insurance, or export credit, agencies.
"Such a network would...make it possible to support the development of export credit agencies in developing economies," he said.
He said a number of countries including the United States, Australia, Canada, the Philippines, Indonesia, South Korea, Thailand and Chile had announced they would participate.

In the interview with Reuters, Sato defended Japan's Individual Action Plan, which fell short of moves to open rice and other farm markets, saying that members agreed in last year's APEC Osaka meeting to exclude farm trade from the action plans.

On U.S. proposals to scrap tariffs on computers and other information technology products, Sato said Japan and the United States had firmly agreed on the plan, called the Information Technology Agreement (ITA). ITA is to be submitted at the World Trade Organisation meeting in Singapore next month.
"But just because Japan and the United States agreed on the ITA, we should not push it too strongly here (at APEC), because we might invite the suspicion of other members," Sato said.
China's WTO entry was also gaining support among APEC's 18 members, Sato said.
"This is gaining support and if China clearly declares its intention, we can probably see a decision at Singapore," Sato said.
Sato said WTO arbitration on trade disputes would be the exception, not the rule.
"At times it is important to cool our heads and bring disputes to the WTO," Sato said, referring to a row about U.S. charges that Japan's photographic film market was closed to U.S. products.
"We sometimes become too close in efforts to understand each other. So the WTO mediation is an exception, not a rule," Sato said.
Sato praised Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, whom he met for the first time on Thursday. Sato became trade minister two weeks ago.
"She is a very intelligent, sharp person and is very rational," Sato said. "I look forward to establishing mutual understanding."
